newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW-Australian living wage case outcome.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Australian living wage case outcome.

text.p: Australia's "living wage" case has been decided, with the outcome being a rise of A$10 a week, in line with a range of economists' expectations.

The Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) had asked for three A$20 a week pay increases over the next three years for workers who have failed to negotiate an enterprise bargaining agreement (EBA), and also for an 8.75 percent increase in minimum award pay rates this year.

The government had argued for an A$8 a week rise, and the Reserve Bank had warned that granting of the full claim by the Industrial Relations Commission (IRC) "would imply a marked acceleration of wages growth," adding 1.6 percent to current annual wages growth.

Economists surveyed by Reuters had forecast an outcome of a A$12 a week rise for those not covered by an EBA, with no percentage increase in award wages. Most forecasts were between A$10 and A$12 a week, which economists said would be consistent with maintaining low inflation. A selection of economists' instant reactions to the decision follows.
JOHN EDWARDS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HSBC MARKETS:

"It looks to be an excellent decision. The A$10 is slightly less than we expected. We assume that they have ordered that it be absorbed into over-award payments and we assume the intention to create a uniform minimum rate will not have a big impact on wages growth. The impact on the markets seems to be reasonably favourable."
CRAIG JAMES, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"It is a favourable outcome for the market. In terms of monetary policy implications we have to wait for tomorrow's CPI figures. But broadly it is neutral in terms of monetary policy. If we do get a further slowing in employment growth it raises the potential for a further rate cut. It is not a significant increase -- I suppose what it does encourage people to do is to seek enterprise bargaining agreements with their employers and know that they are not going to get a free ride out of the Industrial Relations Commission."
MICHAEL BLYTHE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"It was a good result from the financial markets' perspective certainly. I think basically low inflation for the next year or so is now locked in. Everyone was expecting around the A$10 to A$12 mark, so it's certainly come in in line with that. So it shouldn't be too much of a surprise. We're certainly looking at running along the bottom of the two to three percent target range for the next year or so."
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST AUSTRALIA:

"It's a good result. We have looked after the low-paid to some extent but with very little macro-economic inflation cost. We have kept wages within the RBA's guidelines. It's a nice, low-inflation outcome."
BILL EVANS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANKING CORP:

"I think it's a good decision. I think we were expecting somewhere between A$8 and A$12, and the concern was that it may have been as high as A$12. So to come in at A$10 is slightly better than market expectations and therefore has been well received."
SUSAN CREIGHTON, CHIEF ECONOMIST ABN AMRO HOARE GOVETT:

"It reinforces the view we have had for quite sometime now that monetary policy settings will be kept steady through the course of 1997. There is some risk that interest rates may be higher as we go into the first half of 1998. But the outlook between now and the end of the year is for moderate accleration in growth, and the underlying inflation rate, particularly on the back of the good news on the wages side, will I think comfortably stay in that 2.0 to 3.0 percent range that the RBA is targeting."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"It's a decison that has to be embraced by markets and people who are keen for labour market reform and labour market deregulation in that it's encouraging the move to that. It's ensuring that the Reserve Bank's inflation objective remains intact. Yet it's still giving a few dollars to the less well paid so that there's not this need for labour market unrest. So it's appeasing the lower paid workers, but at the same time it's embracing the move to a deregulated labour market."
AKIS HARALABOPOULOS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, GIO AUSTRALIA:

"It's a better than expected outcome. The Industrial Relations Commission has taken on board the RBA's thinking on inflation, with an increase along the lines of what the ACTU was arguing being detrimental to inflation, which is a very encouraging development. There is less pressure now on the RBA to increase official interest rates. Whereas we were thinking of an increase at the end of this year, most analysts will be defering the timing of that increase."
